title: A Norwegian Adventure
paragraphs: I did a three-month clinical clerkship at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (hereafter NTNU) in Trondheim, Norway. I am the third student dispatched from the Nagoya University School of Medicine to NTNU. I wished to do my clerkship in Norway because I wanted to experience Nordic medical care, completely different from Japan, in the nature-rich country of Norway. First of all, I must say that this study abroad in Norway has become a lifelong treasure for me. Without doubt, it has entered the highlights of my life. I was able to have a truly wonderful time and am very satisfied. Since I have now been given the opportunity to convey my experience as a "message from an exchange student," I would like to introduce the experiences during my study abroad as far as I can think of them now.

For many Japanese, Norway is probably a completely unfamiliar country. I was no exception, and I remember that just before the flight I became tremendously anxious, wondering "Can I really live for three months in the unknown land of Norway?" I had gone on overseas trips with friends during vacations several times, but each time I had complained of some kind of poor health, so my family and friends were quite worried about my health for this study abroad. As a result, I received more medicine, warm clothing, food, heat packs than necessary, and even an electric portable massager, and my suitcase became full. After I had checked in the heavy suitcase and said a reluctant goodbye to my family who had come to see me off at the airport, I went through the departure gate. Once through the gate there is no choice but to go forward, so the negative feelings disappeared completely and my expectations for life abroad rose. Until arriving in Trondheim, I had transits in Singapore and Copenhagen. It was physically hard in parts, but I got to travel two countries cheaply and quickly before going to Norway. Before going to a freezing land, I felt it was the best deal to detox from the cold in Singapore.

In the clinical clerkship, I was looked after for one month each in cardiology, medical oncology and pulmonology. Before introducing the clerkship in each department, I would like to summarise what I noticed and felt about the hospital and the healthcare system. All the clerkships were done at St. Olav's Hospital, the hospital affiliated with NTNU. This hospital has separate buildings for each department, and all the buildings are connected by corridors and underground passages. Unlike at Nagoya University Hospital, there was no long wait for elevators to go up to the wards at all, but because it is spread out horizontally, the distances between wards were long. It is so wide that people use scooters to move between wards. I also used one for getting around, and while I felt a slight sense of guilt riding a scooter inside a hospital, it was quite comfortable and pleasant and a fresh experience. Incidentally, this scooter goes quite fast, and I thought it was properly dangerous. Also, at the hospital I received guidance in English not only from the doctors but from all the medical staff, such as nurses, laboratory technicians and radiographers. Norway has one of the highest rates of English use among countries where English is not the mother tongue, and apart from elderly people, almost everyone can speak English fluently. For that reason, I think it was a very easy environment to learn in, also in terms of language. Finally, let me introduce the Norwegian healthcare system. In Norway, patients cannot go to a large hospital without a referral from a Fastlege (family doctor). The Fastlege judges whether one should visit a large hospital or a specialised medical institution. This prevents excessive demand for medical care and makes it possible to use limited medical resources efficiently.

(1) Cardiology I first trained in cardiology. In Norway in February the sun rises late, and at about 8 o'clock when the conference started it was still pitch dark, and when I thought the birds had begun chirping noisily during the conference and looked outside, the sun was starting to rise. The sun also sets early, going down after 16:00, so it became a life in which I entered the hospital while it was dark and left the hospital after it got dark, hardly seeing the sun. Many times I went to school pressing down the snow so as not to slip, in snow and extreme cold I had never experienced before. The otherworldly feeling, just as expected, made my heart leap. Cardiology is in an acute-phase ward called "Akutten og Hjerte Lunge-Senteret," which includes cardiology and pulmonology. On the roof there is a helipad, said to be used when transporting highly urgent patients from remote areas of Norway, and my impression was that doctor helicopters are used more frequently than in Japan. My boss was Dr. Rune, who specialises in the field of heart failure. Dr. Rune was careful in his teaching, very humorous, and very popular among the local students. I went to Dr. Rune's office every day, and he spent such enjoyable time with me that I could no longer tell whether I was going to study or to chat with him. Clerkship hours were from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and in the morning I mainly went with Dr. Rune to hear from the patients on the ward. In the afternoon, Dr. Rune made appointments for me with the sections of cardiology that had procedures, and I observed the echocardiography lab, the angiography lab and pacemaker implantation surgery. Everyone was interested in me, who had come from Japan, and explained the patients and procedures and chatted with me. They also answered my questions readily. What stayed with me among the afternoon procedures was observing coronary stenting in the angiography lab. With the patient conscious, I was allowed to watch up close, taking great care of the sterile field. After the procedure, they explained how the catheter had moved inside the blood vessel, showing me with the catheter actually used. It was not something one can study at a desk, so it was very interesting. Also, after the procedure, the patient noticed that I was clearly not Norwegian and spoke to me. When they learned that I was there from Japan for a clerkship, they said, laughing, "Well, welcome! You can study more on my body!" At that time, the clerkship had just begun and there were many unfamiliar things, but I was very happy that the patient showed a tolerant attitude toward the presence of a Japanese medical student. When I said, "Thank you. Then may I try inserting the catheter next time?", they laughed and shook their head. Every Friday, cake was placed in the ward's break room, and after the day's work the medical staff of the ward could gather in the break room and chat. I too went to the break room to eat cake with Dr. Rune every Friday. Doctors and nurses gathered one after another in the break room to eat cake. While enjoying cake and coffee, we got excited talking about weekend plans and so on. Here too, Dr. Rune kept making humorous remarks and enlivening the place. I thought it is no exaggeration to say that the atmosphere of this ward is created by Dr. Rune. Both doctors and nurses seemed to be able to perform their daily work with composure of mind. I came to want to become a doctor who can value casual communication with medical staff so that I can create a harmonious workplace environment where all the medical staff can work as one.

(2) Medical oncology After saying goodbye to Dr. Rune, in March I trained in medical oncology. This year seemed to be a mild winter, and in March the snow melted and gave a premonition of the arrival of spring. To Norwegians, it seems that in order to enjoy winter the period when snow piles up needs to be of a certain length or more, and they said sadly that they wished it had piled up more. Medical oncology handles cancers of each organ and is divided into groups by organ. In the first week I trained in the endocrine and breast cancer group, in the second week in the gastrointestinal group, and in the third week in the urology group. In the first week in the endocrine and breast cancer group, I observed the rounds and outpatient clinic of the doctor who instructed me. The most shocking was the first day. On the first day of the clerkship in this group, the doctor was explaining the present illness of the patients in her charge and the composition of the chemotherapy regimens currently being given. When we came to the story of prescribing narcotics for pain relief, she said "I cannot prescribe it yet, though," so I asked, "How long after becoming a doctor can one prescribe?" Then, hearing "I am still a student," I nearly went mad. She was a sixth-year student at NTNU who was doing an internship in medical oncology. NTNU has nothing like the so-called polyclinic 2, and instead each student applies for internships on their own. I could not hide my surprise at the high level of a medical student in the same year. The level was so high that I had mistaken her for a supervising doctor. And so began a stimulating week in which I continued to be strongly made to think that I had to work harder. In the clerkship in this group, I performed neurological examinations every day on a patient from breast cancer who was at risk of brain metastasis. I had studied the neurological field for the OSCE and the national exam, but there were parts I had half forgotten, so I reviewed right away. The discussion of estimating the site of brain damage from abnormal neurological findings was clinical and very educational. In the second and third weeks, I saw far more patients than in the first week. In the clerkship in the gastrointestinal group in the second week, in addition to rounds and outpatient clinic, I took part in many conferences. They kindly held the conferences in English for my sake. What strongly remains in my memory from the conferences is the discussion of a patient who had developed liver cancer from hepatitis C. In Norway, it seemed that being infected with hepatitis C itself was rare. So I was asked about the prevalence of hepatitis B and C viruses in Japan and Asia, but I could only answer vaguely, and the doctors cared even about the numbers, asking about how many people. I felt frustrated, thinking that if I could have answered crisply there, I might have taken part too and the discussion might have become more lively. In my studies I had not paid much attention to the epidemiological side, but after this exchange I thought that in my future study I would study the epidemiology of each disease as well as its pathophysiology and treatment. In the clerkship in the urology group in the third week, what left an impression was performing digital rectal examination on patients with prostate cancer. I had done this on a model in the OSCE clerkship, but it was my first time doing it in a real clinical setting. I was happy that as I repeated it, I became able to distinguish the location and hardness of tumours. I am very grateful to the doctors and patients for their cooperation.

(3) Pulmonology For the last month, after the Easter holidays, I trained in pulmonology. In April, the hours of daylight became much longer, and I was surprised that it was still light at 21:00. Even though the sky looked completely like spring, the temperature was still going back and forth around below freezing. In pulmonology, the department was divided into a tumour group and a non-tumour group, and I spent my time going back and forth between the two. What especially stayed with me in this month was bronchoscopy. The pulmonology department at NTNU performs bronchoscopy every day, and I went to the bronchoscopy room every day. They did not do the throat anesthesia before the examination that is done in Japan, and performed the examination with sedation by anesthesia and anesthesia through the bronchoscope. It was impressive that the nurses in the bronchoscopy room performed anesthetic induction and part of the bronchoscope operation. The bronchoscopes in Norway, as in Japan, are made by OLYMPUS, and I unexpectedly encountered a Japanese brand. By observing every day, I came to be able to tell which side, left or right, and which number the bronchoscope was at the moment. Even though I observed every day and reviewed by comparing with photographs, once the branches got finer I could not follow at all, and I felt I still needed to study the anatomy of the bronchi. Perhaps as a result of observing every day, in the last week I was allowed to hold the bronchoscope and practise operating it. It was my first time operating a bronchoscope on a real patient and I was nervous, but since I had only practised with models and simulations, it was a very good experience. On the ward, I was mainly instructed by Dr. Elena. On the ward, we did the doctor's patient rounds and treatment discussions, and when there was a patient who could speak English, I was allowed to take the initial history. I also challenged myself to take blood gases. The needle did not go in on the first try, but the patient also lent me their arm, saying "You must keep trying until he succeeds, for his confidence." I was able to build up plenty of blood-drawing practice before becoming a junior resident, and it was very good practice. Every Thursday after school, Dr. Elena took me to classical concerts that she strongly recommended. I had not a shred of culture regarding classical music, but before I knew it I was listening intently to the music. There were also performances of familiar pieces such as Dvorak's "From the New World," and I was unexpectedly made aware of the goodness of classical music.

(1) Dormitory I lived for three months in a student dormitory about 20 minutes by bus from the hospital. The student dormitories are run by an organisation called Sit (the Student Welfare Organization), and their locations and forms vary. I lived in a nine-storey dormitory in Moholt. Fifteen students lived on each floor, and it was among the largest of the student dormitories in Moholt. (Because it is large and located in the centre of Moholt, it is commonly called the "tower" among students.) The kitchen and living room were shared and the bathroom was private, and it was a comfortable dormitory that was easy to live in. What surprised me most about the building was that the doors are automatic. This applies not only to the dormitory but to most buildings in Norway. The key is not the kind inserted into a keyhole as often seen in Japan but the kind where you hold an IC chip up, and when it responds the door opens automatically. Probably it is a measure to prevent doors from not opening because snow has piled up, but it felt somehow futuristic and exciting. On the floor where I lived, besides Norwegians, there were German, Turkish, Sri Lankan and Mexican students, and I could come into contact with the cultures of various countries. As mentioned above, the kitchen was shared, so I could have pleasant conversations with whichever members happened to be in the kitchen at the right time during cooking or mealtimes. They sometimes made dishes I had never seen in Japan, and just watching them was interesting. The characteristic of this dormitory, above all, is that there are many people and it is lively. After school and on days off, everyone in the dormitory sometimes gathered for parties. Besides those held by the members of the floor alone, I also experienced what is called a "tower party," held by the whole dormitory building. The parties, with people gathered from various countries, were talking cheerfully, dancing and singing..., livelier than I had imagined, and at first I almost felt daunted. I had thought I had experienced lively parties in my university life so far, but by the standard of overseas students, I reflected that perhaps they had not been lively enough. When it was time to return home, the members of the dormitory also held a farewell party for me, and I was able to make very happy memories. Also, right in the middle of Moholt there was a student shared space called Loftet. It is a facility that any student living in Moholt can use free of charge, and in addition to a library and study spaces, there were free drinks, a billiards table, musical instruments, video games and so on, a place in very high demand among students. I too went to Loftet in my free time after school with my laptop to look things up and study. With students I met there and hit it off with, I was able to interact by talking about ourselves and playing Winning Eleven on a PlayStation. In Moholt I was able to lead a comfortable life while enjoying interaction with many students.

(2) Food The hardest thing in life in Norway was food. Since I live alone anyway, I thought I had the cooking skills necessary to live. Furthermore, since I had brought food from Japan, I thought I would not be in trouble at first. However, after I began life in Norway, my days became ones of making and eating pasta that was not tasty at all. Prices are high in Norway and one cannot casually eat out, so I had to keep eating unappetising pasta. While I was making unappetising pasta, the members of the dormitory were making dishes with delicious smells, which made me sad. For a while I despaired of my diet and saw nothing but darkness ahead, but someone who worried about my diet sent me a small rice cooker and rice, and I gratefully relied on it and led a life of eating rice. When the rice cooker and rice arrived at the dormitory, I was struck with shock and cried out with joy. In the end, apart from the first week, I had no trouble at all with food. Thinking that I must enjoy Norwegian food too, I frequently went to supermarkets (mainly REMA 1000). There are not as many delicious things as in Japan, but Norwegian salmon, brown cheese, fruit, juice, chocolate and the like were delicious and I ate them many times. In Norway there is a weekly custom regarding food of eating tacos on Friday night. Following this, I also ate tacos on Fridays, at the hospital and in the dormitory. According to the original custom it is Friday dinner, but since the hospital canteen served Norwegian tacos for lunch, I ate Norwegian tacos with the doctors at lunch. They welcomed me, saying "Once you start eating tacos on Fridays, you have joined the Norwegians." It was funny that the canteen's Friday menu was tacos without fail every week. In the dormitory too, sometimes at dinner a Norwegian floormate made tacos and treated us. One can put as many ingredients as one likes on the tortilla, and I was able to enjoy very satisfying tacos. When we ate tacos together, they always showed a Viking movie in the living room. The history of the Vikings is quite deep and has dark parts, and it made for a heavy dinner time.

(3) Friendships During my stay in Norway, I was able to make friends with many students besides the floormates in my dormitory. I belong to a circle called MDEC, which interacts with students who come to study abroad at the Nagoya University School of Medicine, and I first met again Mari, a student of NTNU I had met there. Mari showed me around the campus and also introduced me to other medical students who were studying abroad at the same time. Introduced like this, I deepened friendships by eating ramen and going out for drinks with a French medical student I became friendly with. One weekend they invited me to a cabin trip to a mountain cabin on the outskirts of Trondheim. On the cabin trip, I was able to have experiences I had never had before, such as walking on a frozen, snow-covered lake and in the forest, a candle night and a Finnish sauna, and I was very satisfied. My personal highlight of the cabin trip was the Finnish steam sauna, going out of the sauna room heated by feeding it firewood and jumping into the snow or into a lake with the ice broken to cool down, which is a truly good memory. Mari also invited me out several times in private. We had a taco party at Mari's home, went to karaoke, and she took me to a sauna. The time I went to the sauna with Mari and the others was April, and the snow had melted, but to cool down I jumped into the sea at Trondheim. It was cold, but it felt absolutely great. In April, Sunniva, whom I had become friendly with through MDEC, came back to Trondheim from Nagoya University. Sunniva also helped me prepare to return home, and we went to parties and studied in the library together. What I remember most is going to eat Norwegian sushi together. Sushi is apparently very popular in Norway too, and I was looking forward to seeing what ingredients there would be. Sushi overseas is mostly so-called rolls, and there were strange combinations such as strawberry and fried shrimp and tuna and fried nori, but I was surprised that all of them tasted good. While eating sushi, a friend of Sunniva pointed out that I was not holding my chopsticks correctly, and it made me think that as a Japanese I must correct the way I hold chopsticks. I am connected on social media with the friends I made during my study abroad and still sometimes get in touch with them. It is not a distance at which we can easily meet, but I hope to see them again someday.

Using long vacations and weekends, I went to various places. Since I had never been to Europe or Scandinavia before this study abroad, travelling was also one of my pleasures. The aurora and fjords I saw on trips within Norway were spectacular, and their splendour left me speechless. I will never forget the night I saw the aurora dance vividly and fantastically overhead. At Easter and after the clerkship ended, I travelled to the UK, Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands and Italy with friends who, like me, were studying in Europe from Nagoya University. Since I had come to Norway alone and hardly had contact with Japanese people, travelling with friends I felt comfortable with while talking about episodes from our study abroad was a good change of mood and a wonderful time.

Now that I am back in Japan, the three months, which had felt long during my stay, feel as if they were a moment. I think I spent such fulfilling days that I forgot the passage of time. These three months were an adventure every day. Each time I found something new my heart raced, and gradually I was enchanted by the city of Trondheim and the country of Norway. The country of Norway, which was a completely unknown realm before I went, has become a familiar and beloved country now. The silvery sky that makes it snow every day, the colourful groups of buildings typical of the Nordic countries, the grand and beautiful nature typified by the fjords, and the well-built Norwegians who recall the Vikings. I came to love everything about Norway. I strongly hope to visit again someday (preferably in summer). In the clinical clerkships in the three departments, I was able to spend a dense time that could not be achieved through desk study or clerkships at Nagoya University. What I learned from interacting in English with hospital staff and sometimes with patients will be useful in my future life as a doctor. Also, being able to come into close contact with real clinical practice in Norway, a country with a well-developed healthcare system, was a valuable life experience. When we said goodbye at the end, Dr. Rune said, "Masa, think carefully about what you work for." Norwegians apparently have a strong impression that Japanese work too much, and he said that I should not be obsessed only with working, but spend time on various things and enrich my own life. I feel that this viewpoint is something like a national character common not only to Dr. Rune but to Norwegians as a whole. I intend to work hard and continue to improve as a doctor from next year, and I thought I should not forget his words "Put first priority on your own life" and the national character of theirs that I tasted in Norway. I understood through my contact with Norwegians that this mindset of Norwegians is directly connected to their high level of happiness, above all else. I will keep the lessons I gained from life in Norway, the Norwegian mindset, safely in a corner of my mind. And when I hit some wall and become troubled, I would like to look back on these three months while thinking of far-off Norway. Because I feel that the memories that shine forever will surely give me strength.

For this dispatched study abroad, I was helped by many people: Dr. 長谷川, the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, the doctors who lectured at the pre-departure training, the seniors who gave me advice, and my family and friends. I would like to take this opportunity to express my heartfelt gratitude to everyone who gave me great support. Thank you very much indeed.
